transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2025-07-08
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Aisha Patel (Polaris Head of ML), Tom Nguyen (Polaris Platform Eng), Lena Brooks (Polaris Security)

Summary:
Quick technical deep dive on prefix/prompt caching: hit-rate expectations, cache key design, multi-tenant safety, consistency with KV cache, batching impacts, quantization implications and VPC/on-prem constraints for private deployments. Decision: run a 1-week pilot with production-like traffic; share detailed design doc and benchmark plan.

Topics:
- Cache key surface and normalization
- Tenant isolation and encryption
- Eviction policies and TTLs for prefix caches
- Effect of batching and KV cache on latency
- Quantization and correctness risks
- VPC/on-prem networking and KMS integration

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Alright thanks everyone for taking the time. we wanted to do a quick deep dive on prefix caching, hit rates, and multi-tenant safety. Diego's gonna lead the tech bits. Aisha, Tom, Lena, you all good?
[00:14] Aisha Patel: Yeah thanks Maya. we're especially worried about correctness — if we cache prefixes will we see hallucinations or stale context; also our PII rules need to be respected.
[00:28] Diego Ramos: Totally. Quick agenda: define cache key, normalization, tenant scoping, TTLs, interactions with KV cache and batching. also talk about pilot plan and metrics — hit rate, tail latency, quality delta.
[00:42] Tom Nguyen: Sounds good. also curious how this works in our VPC deployment — we can't have shared Redis in your cloud, so how do you handle cache locality?
[00:56] Diego Ramos: Good call. For Redwood Private we support customer-hosted cache backing — you can use your Redis or memcached inside the VPC; we integrate with your network via peering and can use KMS for encryption at rest. For Hosted we use an internal multi-tenant cache with tenant namespace keys and per-tenant encryption.
[01:12] Lena Brooks: When you say per-tenant encryption, do you manage keys or can we bring our own KMS?
[01:20] Maya Chen: BYOK supported for Private; for Dedicated we can also integrate with customer KMS via HSM-backed keys. we'll include the network diagram in the doc.
[01:35] Aisha Patel: Back to cache keys — what's the canonical key? prompt prefix text? hashed? do you include model id, temperature, tokens, system prompt etc?
[01:50] Diego Ramos: Good question. Our recommendation is to compose the key from: model identifier + model config fingerprint (quantization/precision + decoding params) + normalized prefix text hash + tenant id + optional route id. Normalization includes whitespace trimming, lowercasing where appropriate, and canonicalizing unicode; but we warn against aggressive normalization that removes semantic differences.
[02:06] Tom Nguyen: Wait, do you hash the prefix? we have prefixes of 4k tokens, hashing might be expensive.
[02:12] Diego Ramos: Typically we compute a SHA-256 over the normalized prefix; it's computed once at request ingress. cost is negligible compared to model inference. we also store prefix length and a short prefix fingerprint to enable partial matches.
[02:30] Aisha Patel: Partial matches? can you explain.
[02:33] Diego Ramos: Sure. e.g., if customer sends a prompt that extends a cached prefix, we look up the longest matching cached prefix key and warm the KV cache. This reduces decoding time but needs careful consistency — we must ensure tokenization boundaries align and that the model config is identical.
[02:50] Maya Chen: That's where hit rate metrics come in — we measure exact key matches and longest-prefix matches; both matter for throughput. In many LLM chat apps we've seen 30-60% effective token-level savings when prefixes are stable.
[03:06] Aisha Patel: Our prefixes change a lot per user — system prompts are stable, but user personalization introduces churn. any suggestions for multi-tenant using shared caches?
[03:17] Diego Ramos: For multi-tenant safety we recommend namespaced keys (tenant id plus key) and per-tenant quotas/eviction classes. Also encrypt entries with tenant-bound keys so one tenant can't read another's cached content even in a shared store. In Hosted mode we rotate per-tenant encryption keys and log access.
[03:36] Lena Brooks: If data is encrypted per-tenant, does that preclude cross-tenant dedupe? we worry about cost savings if we can't dedupe identical prefixes across tenants.
[03:44] Diego Ramos: There's a tradeoff. You can opt into a shared dedupe pool where prefixes are hashed with a global salt — but that requires legal/consent decisions. For strict data separation you can use tenant-only caches.
[03:58] Tom Nguyen: Regarding eviction and TTLs — what are defaults and can we tune per route?
[04:05] Diego Ramos: Defaults: TTL 24h for system prefixes, 1h for user-specific prefixes; LRU eviction at the shard level. We expose per-route configs in Redwood Console so you can set TTLs, max entries, and eviction policy (LRU, LFU, TTL-first). For pilot we'd recommend conservative TTLs and monitor hit-rate.
[04:22] Aisha Patel: How do batching and KV cache interact? if you batch multiple requests, does cache lookup happen per-request or per-batch?
[04:30] Diego Ramos: Cache lookup is per-request at ingress before batching — we compute the key per request and then if there's a cached KV state we can batch requests that share the same warmed prefix. Batching can actually increase effective throughput for cached prefixes because multiple requests share the same KV cache state and avoid repeated prefix decoding.
[04:51] Maya Chen: Note that batching adds tail latency considerations; we have adaptive batching that respects per-request latency SLOs. for pilot we'll capture p50/p95/p99 with and without cache hits.
[05:03] Aisha Patel: Any gotchas with quantized models? we're running int8 for cost reasons.
[05:09] Diego Ramos: Important point. Cache keys must include quantization profile and kernel selection flags; quantization can slightly change tokenization behaviour in edge cases, and depending on model and quantization method, decoding outputs may differ slightly. We test with a quality harness on a subset of prompts to ensure regression within threshold.
[05:27] Tom Nguyen: So if we change quantization or reprovision a different model variant, cached entries become invalidated automatically?
[05:33] Diego Ramos: Yes — model fingerprint changes cause cache miss; we recommend versioned model identifiers to avoid silent surprises. Also we provide metrics on cache invalidation rates tied to model version changes.
[05:46] Lena Brooks: About logs and audit — can we see who accessed which cache entry? for compliance we need an audit trail.
[05:54] Diego Ramos: We emit cache access logs with tenant id, key hash, and access time. In Private mode logs can be routed to your SIEM. We don't log raw prefix text for privacy unless you explicitly enable audit capture; default is hash-only.
[06:10] Aisha Patel: Are there any attacks we should be worried about — cache poisoning or side-channels?
[06:16] Diego Ramos: Cache poisoning is mitigated by strict validation of keys and per-tenant namespaces. For risk of cross-tenant inference attacks we recommend per-tenant encryption and optional per-entry MACs. Side-channels are low but possible; we run constant-time key lookups and restrict metadata exposure in hosted env.
[06:33] Maya Chen: Let's talk success metrics for the pilot — hit rate targets, latency reduction, and quality delta.
[06:40] Diego Ramos: Proposed metrics: token-level hit rate >= 25% baseline, p95 latency improvement >= 15% on cached paths, and model output quality delta < 1% on our eval set. We'll instrument with our tracing and quality hooks to correlate cache hits with quality.
[06:56] Tom Nguyen: For the pilot, what's the minimum traffic volume you need?
[07:00] Diego Ramos: We'd like ~100k tokens/day over a week to get stable hit-rate signals; fewer is ok but noisier. For internal benchmarking we can replay your sample traffic too.
[07:12] Aisha Patel: Ok for PII — we need to guarantee that cached prefixes won't retain PII beyond our policy. How do you handle redaction and token-level masking?
[07:22] Diego Ramos: We recommend sanitizing prefixes at the app layer before caching: remove user-specific PII. Additionally, in Private deployments you can configure a pre-cache scrubber that applies regexes or ML-based PII detectors. Redwood can provide a default scrubber, but customers can provide their own.
[07:40] Lena Brooks: Can scrubbers run in our VPC so data never leaves?
[07:43] Maya Chen: Yes that's the recommended pattern: run scrubbers inside your VPC, write only sanitized prefixes to the cache. If you want us to run scrubbers in hosted mode, we have a contractual add-on and logging controls.
[07:56] Tom Nguyen: On the instrumentation side, what do you need from us to run the benchmark?
[08:00] Diego Ramos: Sample traffic (anonymized), model configs, target routes, and latency SLOs. Also tell us which routes are high-priority for caching. We'll provide a benchmark harness and a small script to replay traffic.
[08:12] Aisha Patel: Any examples of prefix strategies that worked well for other customers?
[08:16] Diego Ramos: One customer segmented: system prompts as long-lived cache items, per-company templates at mid TTL, and user-initialization tokens cached briefly. They saw 45% token savings on system-heavy workflows. We'll share an anonymized case study.
[08:32] Maya Chen: We'll attach the case study and the design doc. any remaining security questions?
[08:37] Lena Brooks: one: how do you protect the cache backing store credentials in Redwood-hosted setups?
[08:43] Diego Ramos: We store creds in a secrets manager encrypted with HSM-backed keys. Access is RBAC protected and audited. For Private you bring your own secrets and we never see plaintext.
[08:58] Aisha Patel: timeline: after you send the doc we expect to set up pilot next week. is that feasible?
[09:04] Maya Chen: yes. Diego can generate the benchmark plan and I'll send the design doc by Thursday.
[09:10] Diego Ramos: I'll also include a sample Redis schema and key naming convention, plus a small test harness to run locally or in your VPC.
[09:17] Tom Nguyen: One more network question: TLS termination for cache traffic — do you support mutual TLS between your service and our cache?
[09:24] Diego Ramos: mTLS supported for Private and Dedicated; Hosted uses TLS with cert pinning; we'll include detailed network and firewall rules in the doc.
[09:34] Maya Chen: Great. let's summarize next steps.
[09:37] Maya Chen: Action items: Maya send docs, Diego draft benchmark and test harness, Polaris share sample traffic and PII policy, Lena confirm VPC/KMS constraints.
[09:50] Aisha Patel: Sounds good. thanks everyone.
[09:53] Maya Chen: Thanks all. We'll follow up with a confluence link and a calendar invite for the pilot kickoff.

End of transcript.
